cards.text: Psalm 95 opens with an invitation, and the psalmist did NOT bring his indoor voice. Come, he tells God's people, let us sing for joy to the LORD and shout to the Rock of our salvation. No humming politely in the back row, friend, we are SHOUTING.

cards.question: The psalmist calls God's people to enter the LORD's presence with ___ and to make a joyful noise to Him in song.
All this singing and shouting has a reason. Who does the psalmist say the LORD is?

answers.text: A great King above all gods
A mighty warrior at the gate
A wise judge over the nations

cards.text: Then the psalmist shows how big this King is: the depths of the earth are in His hand, the mountain peaks belong to Him, and the sea is His. Meanwhile I spent years in ONE junk drawer, and I didn't even own THAT.

cards.question: The psalmist says the sea belongs to the LORD because He ___ it.

cards.text: Then comes a second invitation, O come, and now the psalmist calls the LORD our Maker, the One whose hands formed the sea and the dry land. Those hands made MOUNTAINS, friend, and my hands are a mustache that makes cookies on a good day.

cards.question: The psalm started with shouting and singing. Now how does the psalmist call God's people to come before the LORD their Maker?
The psalmist says the LORD is our God, and we are the people of His pasture, the ___ under His care.
The picture of sheep in the LORD's pasture means God's people are on their own to find food and safety.

cards.text: Then, halfway through verse 7, the whole mood flips with "Today, if you hear His voice," and a warning. It's like a group chat full of party emojis, until somebody types, "Hey. Can we talk?"

cards.question: The warning starts with Today, if you hear His voice. What does it tell God's people not to do?

cards.text: The warning points back to Meribah and Massah, where the Israelites had no water, quarreled with Moses, Israel's leader, and tested the LORD by asking whether He was among them or not (Exodus 17:1-7). Running dry makes everybody cranky, friend, and the dead batteries I shared that drawer with argued about it every single day.

Now listen close, because the voice in the psalm changes: God Himself starts speaking, and He says that there, your fathers tested and tried Him. The LORD just took the mic, friend, and I'm standing up STRAIGHT and fixing my apron.

cards.question: God says the fathers tested and tried Him at Massah because they had never seen His work.

cards.text: I can't point fingers, friend: I've watched my oven bake ten thousand perfect batches, and I STILL crack the door every two minutes to check on it. Now God tells how He felt about that generation, and for how long.

cards.question: God says He was angry with that generation for ___ years, and He said they are a people whose hearts go astray.
God says that generation had known His ways.

cards.text: So God swore an oath in His anger about that generation. Friend, no jokes on this one. This is the most serious line in the whole psalm.

cards.question: What did God swear about that generation?

answers.text: They will never enter His rest
They will never see His face
They will never build His house

findings.problem: This is a who question, but the distractor "A mighty warrior at the gate" is an invented description rather than an identifiable detail from elsewhere in the Bible.

rule.text: For who, which thing and where questions, wrong answers are real details from somewhere in the Bible, like Joppa when the right answer is Tarshish.

findings.problem: The card cites only Psalm 95:6, but it also retells verse 5's statements about the sea and dry land and reaches back to the mountain peaks in verse 4. Its citation is narrower than the material it uses.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: Nothing in the earlier cards gives a clue to the number of years. The baker can only guess an unseen number rather than reason out the blank's meaning.

rule.text: The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: Cards 16, 17 and 19 refer only to "that generation" without identifying which generation within the question. Each question therefore depends on context from cards that are no longer on screen.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.
